metadata.title: Chemotherapy-Induced Nausea and Vomiting: Developing Drugs for Prevention Guidance for Industry: Draft Guidance for Industry
metadata.topic: Draft guideline · FDA human drugs and biologics
metadata.legal_basis: FDA Guidance Document (21 CFR 10.115). Guidance states FDA's current thinking and is not binding unless a statute or regulation requires it; the official text governs.

metadata_verification: Source-register metadata; dates and legal status require human verification.
limitations: English rule-based extraction; no GPT or paid API.

candidates.statement: Sponsors developing drugs for the prevention of CINV should consider the following when 71 selecting clinical trial populations: 72
candidates.context: • To support an indication for the prevention of acute, delayed, or acute and delayed nausea 74 and vomiting associated with HEC, patients should receive chemotherapy classified as 75 HEC by the ASCO guidelines, such as cisplatin. 76

candidates.statement: • To support an indication for the prevention of acute, delayed, or acute and delayed nausea 74 and vomiting associated with HEC, patients should receive chemotherapy classified as 75 HEC by the ASCO guidelines, such as cisplatin. 76
candidates.context: Sponsors developing drugs for the prevention of CINV should consider the following when 71 selecting clinical trial populations: 72 • Although ASCO reclassified anthracycline/cyclophosphamide (AC) chemotherapies from 78 MEC to HEC in 2011, AC chemotherapy has been demonstrated to be less emetogenic 79 than other agents classified as HEC (i.e., cisplatin). FDA does not consider data obtained 80 solely from AC chemotherapy–based trials adequate to demonstrate substantial evidence 81 of effectiveness in patients receiving other HEC regimens. Programs including patients 82 treated with AC chemotherapy should include multiplicity-controlled analyses of the 83 primary and secondary endpoints limited to patients receiving non-AC HEC (per ASCO 84 guidelines) to support a demonstration of efficacy for patients receiving HEC. 85

candidates.context: • To support an indication for the prevention of acute, delayed, or acute and delayed nausea 74 and vomiting associated with HEC, patients should receive chemotherapy classified as 75 HEC by the ASCO guidelines, such as cisplatin. 76 • Available data show that drugs demonstrated to be effective at preventing CINV in a 87 population receiving HEC are also effective at preventing CINV in patients receiving 88 MEC. Therefore, FDA may consider approving an indication for the prevention of CINV 89 in patients receiving MEC based on sufficient data to support the safe use of the drug in 90 the MEC population, together with demonstration of effectiveness in adequate and well- 91 controlled trials in patients receiving HEC. 92

candidates.statement: • If an indication for the prevention of CINV in patients receiving MEC is being sought 94 independently, the trial population or populations should receive chemotherapeutic agents 95 classified as MEC by the ASCO guidelines. 96
candidates.context: • Available data show that drugs demonstrated to be effective at preventing CINV in a 87 population receiving HEC are also effective at preventing CINV in patients receiving 88 MEC. candidates.statement: Sponsors developing drugs for the prevention of CINV should consider the following when 105 designing clinical trials: 106
candidates.context: • Patients should receive standard of care background antiemetic therapy in accordance 108 with the ASCO guidelines. These regimens should be protocol-specified, standardized, 109 and given to all patients in both treatment groups to facilitate the interpretation of the test 110 drug’s safety and effectiveness. 111

candidates.context: Sponsors developing drugs for the prevention of CINV should consider the following when 105 designing clinical trials: 106 • FDA recommends a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial design for 113 sponsors that intend to demonstrate superiority of their drug added to standard of care 114 compared with standard of care alone. 115

candidates.statement: • FDA recommends a randomized, double-blind, active comparator trial design for 117 sponsors that intend to demonstrate noninferiority or superiority to an approved therapy. 9 118 Such a trial should include the following arms: 119
candidates.context: • FDA recommends a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial design for 113 sponsors that intend to demonstrate superiority of their drug added to standard of care 114 compared with standard of care alone. 115 – Active Comparator: Standard of care antiemetic prophylaxis (drugs from two to four 121 classes as recommended by ASCO) 122

candidates.statement: • Permitted rescue medications and their administration schedule should be protocol- 128 specified and standardized. 129

candidates.statement: Sponsors developing drugs for the prevention of CINV should consider the following: 133

• Sponsors should prespecify the acute phase (0 through ≤ 24 hours), the delayed phase 145 (>24 through ≤ 120 hours), or acute and delayed phases to define the period or periods 146 for efficacy endpoint assessments, depending on the mechanism of action of the drug and 147 when the primary treatment effects are anticipated. 148
candidates.context: – A secondary endpoint of the absence of nausea, defined as no nausea and no use of 142 rescue antiemetic medication 10 143 • Sponsors may include a secondary endpoint of the assessment of efficacy in the overall 150 phase (onset within 0 through ≤ 120 hours). FDA does not recommend sponsors select 151 the overall phase for primary efficacy assessments, as drugs are often found to be 152 effective for either acute or delayed onset CINV, and this information is needed to inform 153 optimal use. 154

candidates.statement: • To gain precision in evaluating overall treatment effects, FDA recommends that 167 statistical analyses adjust for patient characteristics at baseline that may impact efficacy 168 outcomes, (e.g., younger age, female sex, a history of morning sickness, history of no or 169 low use of alcohol, history of previous chemotherapy, the presence of central nervous 170 system lesions, and history of motion sickness). Sponsors should also consider exploring 171 subgroup analyses and potential treatment interactions based on these factors. 172
candidates.context: • FDA recommends sponsors analyze the primary endpoint (i.e., a binary endpoint defined 161 as no vomiting and no use of rescue antiemetic medication) and secondary endpoint (i.e., 162 a binary endpoint defined as no reported nausea and no use of rescue antiemetic 163 medication) by evaluating the difference in the proportions of responders across 164 treatment arms. 165 • Sponsors should prespecify the approach to ensure tight control of type I error rate when 174 testing multiple endpoints (i.e., primary and secondary endpoints) that are clinically 175 meaningful and for which labeling claims may be of interest. 176

Sponsors should also consider exploring 171 subgroup analyses and potential treatment interactions based on these factors. 172 • If treatment effects are anticipated in both the acute and the delayed phases, these 178 analyses should also be appropriately controlled for multiplicity. 179

candidates.context: • Sponsors should prespecify the approach to ensure tight control of type I error rate when 174 testing multiple endpoints (i.e., primary and secondary endpoints) that are clinically 175 meaningful and for which labeling claims may be of interest. 176 10 Demonstrating significant treatment effect on the primary endpoint of complete response (no vomiting and no use of rescue antiemetic medication) in the absence of a significant treatment effect on the secondary endpoint (no nausea and no use of rescue antiemetic medication) may not be sufficient to support an indication for the prevention of the nausea component of the CINV indication.

candidates.statement: Sponsors developing drugs for the prevention of CINV should consider the following when 186 using clinical outcome assessments (e.g., patient-reported outcome and observer-reported 187 outcome instruments): 188
candidates.context: D. Clinical Outcome Assessments 184 • FDA recommends collecting data related to the severity of the patient’s nausea at its 190 worst during the recall period (e.g., using a verbal rating scale with response options such 191 as none, mild, moderate, and severe), assessing frequency and/or duration of nausea, and 192 assessing impacts of nausea on the patient’s daily living and functioning. The design of 193 the instrument selected (including the specific response options in the questions included) 194 should be informed by qualitative data from patients to demonstrate that the measurement 195 strategy adequately captures patients’ experiences with nausea. 11 196

candidates.context: Sponsors developing drugs for the prevention of CINV should consider the following when 186 using clinical outcome assessments (e.g., patient-reported outcome and observer-reported 187 outcome instruments): 188 • Sponsors should use instruments with daily assessments (e.g., using a recall period of the 198 past 24 hours), and respondents should complete the instruments at the same time each day 199 (e.g., in the evening before bedtime). Instruments should measure the primary endpoint of 200 complete response (i.e., no vomiting and no use of rescue medication) and the secondary 201 endpoint of no nausea and no use of rescue antiemetic medication, using either the same 202 or different instruments for each endpoint. 203
